abstract.p: The growing sophistication of smart buildings has necessitated the use of artificial intelligence (AI), Internet of Things (IoT), and automated fire protection systems to improve safety and operational effectiveness. This paper advances a quantitative safety governance model of an AI-driven fire protection system for smart buildings. In order to evaluate the suggested quantitative safety governance framework, a computational simulation has been created in the R programming language. The simulation engine was run on 10,000 distinct synthetic safety conditions, each of which represented different levels of ambient temperature, smoke density, and hardware reliability. A separate set of 10,000 synthetic three-step trajectories supplied 8,000 training and 2,000 held-out test scenarios. The model utilizes the simulated sensor data, the sensor fusion algorithm, and the deterministic risk scoring technique in an integrated safety index model for the continuous evaluation of the safety of the system. A Random Forest predictor is also included to predict the next-step reliability-adjusted safety index on synthetic trajectories. The governance layer uses examples of safety thresholds and rule-based decision-making to determine the classification of the index defined by the model. The proposed solution aids dynamic model-defined safety evaluation. On a synthetic held-out test set, the model achieved a mean absolute error (MAE) of 0.039592, a root mean square error (RMSE) of 0.049917, and a coefficient of determination ($R^2$) of 0.961849, while achieving 92.55% governance consistency. The effects on reducing false alarms and enhancing response time were not evaluated. The results demonstrate the potential of utilizing AI, quantitative risk modeling, and governance principles in order to take fire safety management in intelligent environments to the next level.

sec.title: 1. Introduction
sec.p: The rise of urbanization and smart buildings has dramatically raised the fire safety complexities of buildings, especially in high-rise, mixed-use and high-density buildings where operational interconnections create a dynamic hazard environment. Smart buildings are cyber-physical computing systems that integrate building management systems (BMS) with Internet of Things (IoT)-enabled equipment (intelligent surveillance, automation of building communication, heating, ventilation, and air conditioning [HVAC] controls, access management) and computer and networking technologies. These technologies enhance building performance, efficiency, sustainability, and occupant comfort, but they also pose new challenges during emergencies, particularly during fire, where timeliness of system interaction is crucial [1], [2], [3].

Smart buildings experience rapid developments during fire events compared to traditional buildings, attributed to dense occupancy, challenges in vertical evacuations, smoke spread via integrated systems, and reliance on automated functions. Though traditional fire safety measures such as smoke detectors, sprinklers, and escape routes are still mandatory as per fire codes (for example, National Fire Protection Association [NFPA] 13 and NFPA 72), the design of these methods is reactive in nature in that they start operating once the fire hazard reaches a threshold. This aggravates firefighting, property damage, and ineffective evacuation in evolving fire scenarios [4], [5]. Moreover, fixed fire alarm systems cannot respond to the dynamic changes of smoke concentration, air interference, temperature change, and occupant distribution, which hampers their adaptability to smart building facilities [4].

According to recent research, a shift from fire protection to proactive fire safety engineering for continuous monitoring, predictive risk assessment, and dynamic response is justified. The current trend of effective fire prevention and protection increasingly relies on incorporating smart fire sensors, evacuation planning in real time, and operational control instead of alarm-only systems [6], [7]. Meng et al. [8] also highlighted integrating management models with early fire detection technologies in a forest-fire suppression context to enable a proactive rather than reactive approach to fire management.

Fire protection systems have greatly improved beyond rule-based systems through the integration of artificial intelligence (AI), IoT, digital twins, and sensor fusion. Computer vision and deep learning models (such as YOLO-based models) enhance fire detection, reduce false alarms, identify smoke and model fire spread [9], [10], [11]. AI models also assist with real-time anomaly detection in industrial IoT [12]. Vision-based methods have been used to monitor fire progression [13]. Digital twins maintain situational awareness via real-time fire simulation and IoT systems with sensors and devices that update the environmental risk status in real time to help accelerate fire emergency decision-making [1], [5], [14].

However, most previous research is relatively focused on detection accuracy rather than governance. Existing studies tend to focus on fire detection accuracy, while less attention is paid to the use of AI outputs, which need to undergo verification, interpretation, and control measures prior to execution of safety-critical decisions such as prioritization of people to evacuate, activation of suppression systems, and allocation of emergency resources. Accurate detection doesn’t necessarily ensure safe decisions in high-risk settings.

AI systems introduce risks of system bias, uncertainty, lack of visibility, over-reliance, data dependency, and accountability confusion in a human-AI system, which are more critical in fire protection operations where the consequences of an operational failure can result in devastating injuries and damage [15]. The European Union (EU) AI Act sets requirements for high-risk AI systems [16]. AI has been studied in safety management across different industries [17]. Building information modeling (BIM) and AI convergence have been studied in construction safety [18]. The available literature also reveals a disconnect between the fast-growing pace of AI adoption and the lagging pace of governance development that can measure and manage the risks in runtime scenarios.

Technical standards related to traditional fire engineering, such as NFPA 13 (Standard for the Installation of Sprinkler Systems), NFPA 72 (National Fire Alarm and Signaling Code), ISO 16732 (Fire Risk Assessment), ISO 23932 (General Principles of Fire Safety Engineering), and governance frameworks such as National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) Artificial Intelligence Risk Management Framework (AI RMF), AI management systems (ISO/IEC 42001) and EU AI Act [16] have an emphasis on accountability, transparency, explainability, and human supervision. However, there is a gap between the two spheres in academic literature. There are not many studies that consider quantifying fire risks using AI, predictive AI, explaining decisions in AI algorithms, and implementing governance-based safety boundaries in the operational framework for intelligent building fire safety monitoring.

This paper bridges this knowledge gap by suggesting a quantitative safety governance model for AI-based fire protection systems in smart buildings. The system uses quantitative fire risk-based assessment, real-time sensor monitoring, sensor fusion, predictive AI models, and governance-based intervention thresholds to establish an integrated model of proactive fire protection. In contrast to traditional fire protection systems that have traditionally focused primarily on detection, the model defines clear safety thresholds and automated and human-oversight-based intervention rules, and predicts fire scenarios to support fire engineering decisions. The predictions evaluated in this study concern synthetic, model-derived indices rather than observed fire events or demonstrated building-level safety outcomes.

This research contributes by transforming the fire protection process from one based on detection efficiency to an efficient and accountable fire protection process that includes predictive analytics combined with governed fire protection process control. This research specifically provides: (1) a comprehensive framework for AI predictions, fire risk assessments, and governance; (2) a governance structure that can set measurable thresholds and boundaries for safety and security; (3) explainable decision-making processes to improve transparency and trust and enable human override; and (4) a governance-based approach that fits well within the smart building management and fire protection engineering requirements.
The framework therefore separates synthetic index calculation and prediction from practical building management, which remains a proposed rather than empirically tested process.

The additional management objectives are to determine which users get model-generated alerts, when human intervention and escalation are needed, and what safeguards prevent the advisory algorithm from affecting independently authorized protective measures.

sec.title: 2.1. Smart buildings and fire protection system complexity
sec.p: The main purpose of smart buildings is to provide more safety, efficiency, and responsiveness in both working and living spaces through incorporation of AI technology, automated building operations, IoT technology, digital twin systems, and BMS [19]. These technologies enhance energy and resource efficiency, sustainability, and human well-being, but they also add to fire protection complexity as issues in one subsystem can quickly propagate, leading to cascading effects during fires [3]. This problem is further compounded in high-rise and mixed-use buildings because of problems associated with vertical transportation, building density, and interconnections between fire protection and building systems.

In smart buildings, fire events exhibit interactions between smoke, ventilation, electrical systems, human psychology and communication systems, which vary over time. This makes assessment tasks, such as early detection, coordination of suppression action and occupant evacuation, more complex. Studies reveal that the ability to prevent fires increasingly relies more on integrated fire mitigation technologies and coordination actions, rather than individual alarm or suppression systems [2], [6].

However, smart building fire systems are still often managed on a subordinate basis, with various fire detection, suppression, alerts and building controls operating in isolation. This is uncoordinated and bottlenecks fire emergency management and response. An example of fire safety management using a digital twin system was provided by Almatared et al. [1], who discussed fire safety visualization and operation awareness, but Yang et al. [20] examined advanced image-based fire detection without validating the governance system studied here. This implies technical advancement for fire detection needs to be supported by holistic system control.

sec.title: 2.2. Limitations of traditional fire safety approaches
sec.p: Current fire safety strategies are primarily passive (i.e. fire alarms and sprinklers, and other risk or hazard mitigation measures) as they are activated when variables exceed a threshold. Smoke alarms and sprinklers are still key components of NFPA 13 and NFPA 72, but their use of threshold and manual controls limits their ability to address rapidly evolving fire risks [4], [9].

One of the main reasons is static risk assessment. Conventional systems cannot provide an on-going assessment of conditions such as the spread of smoke, temperature change, air flow change, and changes in occupant density. This can result in delayed detection of hazards, more false alarms, and unsafe escape routes due to the pre-determined escape plans based on fixed fire scenarios [4], [5]. Meacham [21] advised that performance-based fire safety plans should be based on sociotechnical adaptation rather than a threshold approach.

The latest studies call for a shift towards proactive fire safety engineering that involves real-time monitoring and likelihood-based risk assessment. Meng et al. [8] highlighted combining management models with smart early detection systems in forest-fire suppression for proactive responses. Franchini et al. [22] and Tan et al. [23] also discussed probability-based fire safety design and human and organizational risk factors, respectively, as considerations for decision-making.

sec.title: 2.3. Artificial intelligence, internet of things, and sensor fusion in fire protection
sec.p: Smart buildings have benefited from improved fire detection, prediction and response via AI. AI-based fire detection techniques based on deep learning, including YOLOv8 and other deep learning systems have reported detection performance on their evaluated image datasets [9], [10], [11]. These allow image-based identification of visible smoke or flames.

AI is not only used for fire detection but also for proactive fire safety. Deep learning has been evaluated for forecasting fire development and flashover in reduced-scale compartment fire tests [24]. Desikan et al. [12] also demonstrated how fault-tolerant sensor fusion addresses faulty sensor measurements and anomaly detection in industrial IoT, rather than building-level emergency response.

IoT, distributed sensor networks, and monitoring systems support fire-safety monitoring through environmental sensing and occupancy-related information [14], [25], [26]. In addition, Cicero et al. [27] and Huang et al. [28] studied data-driven anomaly detection in smart buildings and equipment health monitoring in converter-station fire-protection IoT devices, respectively; neither study established reduced building-fire emergency response times.

Likewise, sensor fusion and data platforms enhance fire detection reliability by leveraging multiple data types instead of individual sensor information. Desikan et al. [12] investigated fault-tolerant sensor fusion in industrial IoT, and He et al. [29] evaluated bidirectional long short-term memory (BiLSTM) models for multi-sensor fire detection. But most research continues to focus on improving fire prediction accuracy but not how to define confidence levels and uncertainty to guide decision-making, such as when to trigger suppression systems or when humans should intervene.

sec.title: 2.4. Quantitative risk assessment and governance gap
sec.p: Quantitative Risk Assessment (QRA) offers structured approaches to assess fire risk, severity, uncertainty and safe bounds. Probabilistic models rather than deterministic models are used in this type of evaluation for performance-based fire design, such as in high-rise buildings and industrial plants.

Uncertainty in fires is typically modeled using Bayesian networks, fuzzy logic and simulation. Zhao et al. [30] demonstrated the use of simulation and machine learning in storage-tank fire-risk modeling, while Tan et al. [23] and Nishino [31] showed the relevance of organizational factors and cascading urban-fire hazards, respectively, in their separate settings. Franchini et al. [22] also showed the application of probabilistic approaches to performance-based fire design.

But QRA studies mostly remain focused on hazard assessment rather than deriving risk-based governance-oriented practices. Very few studies provide clear criteria about when to trigger a computer-based intervention or override, and how to attribute liability in intelligent fire protection systems.

sec.title: 2.5. Explainable artificial intelligence and governance in safety-critical systems
sec.p: With increased usage of AI in critical safety domains, there have been growing concerns of transparency, trust, accountability, and overall trustworthiness. For example, in fire protection systems, AI predictions can be used to inform decisions about evacuating people, activating suppression systems, and prioritising emergencies, with errors leading to potentially catastrophic consequences. Thus, while it is important for forecasts to be accurate, it is necessary to also know the reasons behind decisions.

Explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) explains the decisions made by AI systems. XAI can audit, verify, and manage AI models, which black box AI cannot do. Islam et al. [32] discuss explainability in safety-critical applications, whereas Mersha et al. [33] give an overview of explainability methods, evaluation, and challenges in AI applications.

Governance is also essential for successful deployment. The NIST AI RMF and ISO/IEC 42001 framework cover the topic of AI governance, and the EU AI Act [16] provides the regulatory framework for high-risk AI systems. Corrêa et al. [34] and Díaz-Rodríguez et al. [35] also found that, in addition to abstract principles, effective implementation of AI requires governance systems. The official NIST AI RMF and ISO/IEC 42001:2023 provide guidance on general AI risk governance and management systems rather than specific fire alarm activation criteria [36], [37].

However, governance frameworks are rarely created in fire engineering, and many research papers about fire detection overlook explainability and accountability. This leads to a disconnect between efficiency and safety of AI systems.

sec.title: 2.6. Research gap and theoretical positioning
sec.p: Areas such as fire detection, smart building, AI prediction, IoT sensing, sensor fusion, QRA, and AI governance have seen developments in the literature. But these areas are isolated. Fire engineering research improves detection and suppression, while governance research makes it clear that there needs to be transparency and accountability—but not threshold settings for fire protection systems.

We need studies on predicting fire risks, explainable AI modeling, setting governance-based fire protection thresholds, and human-supervised intervention to optimize smart buildings for fire protection. Therefore, AI decision-making and control often do not have thresholds for intervention, accountability, and compliance in safety strategies.

This research fills this gap in knowledge by developing a quantitative safety governance model that brings together deterministic fire risk modeling, AI-based fire prediction models, sensor fusion, transparent safety-index calculations, and governance safety thresholds into a single operational framework. Unlike previous research mostly focusing on detection improvement, this framework particularly stresses measurable, transparent, and accountable safe conditions for practical fire protection in smart buildings. The study uses explicit governance rules but does not apply an XAI method to explain individual Random Forest predictions.

sec.title: 3. Safety governance framework for artificial intelligence-driven fire protection systems
3.1. Concept of safety governance
sec.p: Safety governance is a systematic framework that is aimed at regulating, evaluating, and managing the actions of safety-sensitive systems to ensure that they do not operate beyond an acceptable amount of risk. Safety governance is based on constant monitoring of the system, quantitative assessment, and policy-based decision-making, unlike traditional safety management, where the main focus is on predefined procedures and manual supervision.

In contemporary engineered systems, especially those that are being automated and are also particularly using AI, some decisions involving safety can be made automatically without necessarily requiring human intervention. Thus, it is necessary that we can define a governance model specifying how safety can be evaluated, how decisions can be made and when control actions can be triggered.

In fire protection systems, governance plays a vital role in order to make sure that detectors, suppressors, ventilator systems, and alarms respond in a consistent and stable way. In case of the integration of these systems with the intelligent building platforms, the interactions become more complex, and the formal safety governance framework becomes essential.

Safety governance is mainly aimed at ensuring that the system is kept within a safe operating envelope through the continued evaluation of the existing safety status and a comparison with the established safety limits.

sec.title: 3.2. Safety governance in artificial intelligence-driven fire protection systems
sec.p: The fire protection systems are increasingly becoming more involved in AI to assist in the monitoring, fault detection, and decision-making automatically. The algorithms of AI have the ability to handle different signals from sensors simultaneously and detect unusual patterns, which may indicate a threat of fire. However, automated decision-making brings up several issues, as the response from the system is possible without any verification from the human side.

It is important to have governance in the AI-based fire protection system in order to ensure that the decisions made by the algorithms do not contradict safety needs. In the absence of a governance model, the system can create false alarms, slow reactions, or wrong control measures.
The safety governance framework should therefore establish the following:
• how safety is measured;
• how risk is evaluated;
• how decisions are triggered;
• how control actions are selected.

In the suggested solution, the safety governance is founded on a quantitative safety index, which reflects the present-day state of safety in the fire protection system. This index is determined based on real-time sensor data, system reliability data, as well as AI prediction.
The governance model then compares calculated safety index to predefined safety limits so as to conclude whether the system is working in the Normal, Warning, High Risk or Critical mode.

sec.title: 3.3. Safety variables in smart fire protection systems
sec.p: The safety condition of a smart fire protection system is presented by various variables that characterize the environmental conditions and the work of the system. Sensor networks and BMS are able to provide these variables continuously in smart buildings.
Typical safety variables include:
• temperature deviation,
• smoke concentration,
• airflow condition,
• electrical load level,
• occupancy density,
• equipment status,
• detector reliability,
• suppression system availability,
• communication status.

All these variables will reflect the safety condition of a different aspect. One parameter is not enough to assess the presence of fire risk in multifamily buildings; that is why several variables should be united in one safety measure.
All the variables should be taken to similar scales to ensure that they can be evaluated quantitatively prior to inclusion in the safety index model.

sec.title: 3.4. Definition of safety state
sec.p: Within the framework proposed, the safety state of the fire protection system is determined with the help of the continuous safety index that reflects the current level of operational safety.

The system is not characterized by binary states (safe/unsafe), but several levels of safety are implemented. This enables the model of governance to identify slow yet gradual variations in the condition of the system and to initiate preventive measures prior to a critical condition being attained.
Safety State is categorized under four different levels:
(1) Normal state—system functions within safe bounds
(2) Warning state—abnormal conditions detected
(3) High Risk state—safety margin reduced
(4) Critical state—immediate action required
These levels enable the system to react in progressive stages as opposed to when a fire alarm state is reached.
The safety state incorporates real-time information and AI prediction to constantly update the safety state and enable the governance model to aid in proactive fire protection.

sec.title: 3.5. Structure of the proposed safety governance framework
sec.p: The suggested model of safety governance has four major elements:
(1) Data acquisition module
(2) Safety index calculation module
(3) AI prediction module
(4) Governance decision module
• The data acquisition module gathers real-time data from sensors in the building.
• The safety index module is used to assess the level of safety that is currently present based on a quantitative model.
• The AI module forecasts the safety situation in the future using the existing data.
• The governance module is used to compare the computed safety index to the established limits and identify the necessary control measures.

• This construction is to make sure that automatic fire protection systems work based on established safety regulations and should not be out of range of reasonable risk even in changing circumstances. Independently approved fire protection functions remain separate from the proposed governance module.
• The second part presents the mathematical conceptualization of the quantitative safety index applied in the intended governance model.

In accordance with the decision, control methods such as warning, inspection, or the use of fire protection systems would be verified and escalated as per the approved management process.

The unified framework would hopefully aid in making sure that the fire protection systems developed using AI would remain predictable and adaptive to the environment of the buildings while also aiding in the consideration of preventive measures in time.

sec.title: 5.1. Role of artificial intelligence in safety governance
sec.p: AI plays a vital role in enhancing safety governance within AI-based fire protection systems to ensure constant monitoring, decision-making processes, and predictive analysis. Whereas traditional alarm systems act on predetermined thresholds, AI algorithms can read more than one sensor signal at the same time, detect much more complex patterns, and identify even minor anomalies that could signal possible dangers or unsafe situations. In this study, the fitted model predicts a model-defined index using synthetic histories, not actual fire events; operational effects remain untested.

As discussed in the framework of the proposed safety governance, AI is not a substitute for the quantitative safety index model; on the contrary, it completes it. The safety index, as shown in Eqs. (1)–(4), would give a real-time estimation of the prevailing risk-oriented safety index, whereas the AI module can be used to predict future safety by using past and real-time information. The system is designed to predict changes in a model-defined risk index, as opposed to being just reactive to breaches of the threshold. Eq. (5) is employed to provide the temporal base, whereas the final governance index is provided by Eq. (8).

The framework provides the safety index with predetermined operational limits, which may inform situational awareness and proposed governance measures within model-defined limits in the dynamic building environment. This preventative strategy is proposed; reductions in system failure, false alarms, and response delays require independent field validation.

In order to evaluate the suggested quantitative safety governance framework, a computational simulation has been created in the R programming language. The simulation engine was executed on 10,000 independent synthetic snapshot conditions and a separate set of 10,000 synthetic three-step temporal scenarios. The independent snapshots sample temperature uniformly from 20–100 ℃, smoke from 0–1, and equipment reliability from 0.5–1; the trajectories incorporate defined temporal dependence and perturbations. Random seed = 42; the training set has 8,000 temporal scenarios, and the test set has 2,000 time-step scenarios. sec.title: 6.1. Governance decision concept
sec.p: The important task of the safety governance framework is to make sure that proposed governance decisions follow the model-defined safety limits. In automated and AI-based fire protection systems, some decisions can be made without direct human influence, so it is crucial to provide an organized decision model that will help identify whether the system’s actions are consistent with established safety requirements.

In the proposed structure, the final safety index determined using Eq. (8) is used as the basis to make governance decisions. The decision module constantly contrasts the present safety condition with preset safety thresholds and decides on the corresponding control measure in accordance with the level of risk which is evaluated.

The governance model offers a proposed staged response to model-defined risk based on the level of safety in the present moment as opposed to the traditional fire alarm systems, which react to the presence of a hazard once it is detected. Whether this minimizes actual false alarms or enables earlier physical interventions was not evaluated.

The governance decision framework is intended to work in a continuous mode to update the system state as sensor data is received in real time, with any real-world integration requiring separate safety certification and field validation.

sec.title: 6.2. Safety limits and governance rules
sec.p: Safety limits should be set in order to regulate the functioning of the fire protection system. These limits define acceptable safety-index levels and specify when the system should remain under monitoring or initiate control measures. The model of governance under proposal makes use of the four safety levels as follows:
• Normal level
• Warning level
• High Risk level
• Critical level
Each level corresponds to a different decision rule.

→
Normal level: The system functions normally and requires no intervention but monitoring.

→
Warning level: Abnormal conditions are discovered; further inspection or preventative measures may be necessary.

→
High Risk level: The safety margin is decreased; the protection system must be prepared.

→
Critical level: urgent verification and emergency escalation according to approved site procedures; independent fire-protection functions remain governed by their certified controls.

Each level has some governance policies that control the response of the system. In light of such policies, the structure is set in such a manner that makes it possible for the fire prevention system to be proactive rather than reactive to the situation of emergency. The question is whether this method makes the system reliable or lowers the number of false alarms.

sec.title: 6.4. Control actions in automated fire protection systems
sec.p: The BMS would communicate corresponding advisory measures for staff review in the event that the governance structure establishes what the decision state ought to be. These actions depend on the level of safety the final safety index has reached, subject to independent approved protection procedures and site-specific safety oversight.
Typical control actions include:
• sending warning messages,
• activating inspection procedures,
• adjusting ventilation systems,
• isolating electrical circuits,
• preparing suppression systems,
• activating alarms and sprinklers.

The proposed framework consisting of quantitative safety evaluation and automated controls is meant to enable phased proposed reactions; however, any improvement in the number of false alarms or building safety has yet to be tested in complex and variable situations. sec.p: Proposed fault handling: In the case of any fault in the temperature and smoke data, the advisory module withholds a normal risk clearance and calls for a manual inspection by staff. A communication fault results in a maintenance fault, but existing firefighting functions continue to work separately. sec.title: 7. Case study: application to a smart high-rise building
7.1. Description of the building system
sec.p: To illustrate the proposed safety governance framework, as one of the case studies, a hypothetical 40-story smart high-rise building is considered; the chosen building is an example of an intelligent building of modern times with automated fire safety, distributed sensors, and a building management platform that can monitor and control the building in real time. The floor count and inter-floor smoke dynamics are not independent simulation variables.
The building is presumed to have the following attributes:
• 40 floors
• mixed occupancy (residential and office)
• automatic sprinkler system
• addressable fire detection system
• HVAC smoke control system
• electrical monitoring system
• BMS
• IoT sensor network
Sensors installed in the building provide real-time measurements of:
• temperature
• smoke concentration

In the proposed workflow, measurements would be sent to a safety governance module, where the safety index is calculated using Eqs. (1)–(4) and the integrated governance index is formed by Eq. (8). This is intended to support continuous model-defined safety assessment and proposed decision-making in the AI-based system of governance. An illustrative floor-18 alert would be escalated through a control-room operator to the safety manager; this communication workflow has not been field-tested. In this hypothetical floor-18 example, temperature and smoke sensors on that floor would transmit their measurements through the building monitoring network to the BMS and governance module, which would display the resulting alert to the control-room operator.

sec.title: 7.5. Discussion of case study results
sec.p: The framework is intended to support data-driven proposed decisions based on predetermined safety limits because it will map the final safety index to predetermined safety limits. This could help inform management decisions, but improvements in the stability and reliability of real fire protection systems in complex and dynamic buildings have not been measured.

It is the discussion of the simulated scenarios that illustrates that the framework assigns model-defined levels under the tested synthetic conditions. It is able to differentiate between Normal, Warning, High Risk and Critical states and propose corresponding control measures at each level.

sec.p: This section outlines and describes the work of the suggested safety governance framework depending on the case study scenarios presented in Section 7. The discussion is concentrated on the dynamics of the safety index and its efficiency in grasping the status of operations of AI-based fire protection systems.

The outcomes denote that the offered safety index offers a continuous model-derived depiction of the simulated safety index. In normal circumstances, the calculated value of the safety index fell into the preset Normal range

The safety index showed differences across synthetic scenarios with distinct temperature, smoke and reliability inputs. This illustrates the model-defined differences between safety levels rather than tested early identification of actual building hazards. As a result, the governance rules can recommend proposed measures for elevated model-defined risk levels, subject to future field validation.

Furthermore, the weighted safety index (as defined in Eq. (1)) has been used. The combination of several safety variables into one quantitative metric is made possible by Eq. (1). This multivariate model corresponds to the complexity of fire protection systems of smart buildings where the safety depends on a mixture of environmental, operational, and system-related factors. Compared to traditional systems with a single-threshold alarm system, this approach offers a more detailed and model-defined assessment of the safety of the system.

All in all, the behavior of the safety index as observed indicates that it will be able to aid in continuous monitoring, the proposed interpretation of model-defined risk levels, and informed decision-making of the safety governance framework proposed.

As it follows from the figures obtained within the simulation scenarios, it is possible to state that predicted indices can be classified into specific alert categories, without achieving earlier detection of real fires.

Such predictive capabilities are supposed to reflect the transformation from the reactive approach towards fire protection to proactive risk management. By means of the AI prediction, the decision-making process can suggest measures depending on the level of the predicted index. sec.title: 8.3. Effect of governance decision rules
sec.p: The decision criterion as stated in Eq. (9) is another vital one that allows turning the safety index in Eq. (8) into meaningful decision criteria for the system. This mapping procedure provides an assurance that all the system responses will be in line with the predetermined safety limits to create a consistent and policy-driven safety management approach.

The results from the case studies indicate that the system is characterized by the governance rules system that allows implementing different measures based on the level of safety. For example, in case of the Warning state, the system implements measures such as notifying and inspecting in Warning, whereas Critical corresponds to the measures of urgent verification and independent approval. This is a case-by-case response approach where each case is handled differently depending on its particular level.

This approach to decision-making is very progressive and distinguishes graded model-defined alert levels without overriding certified alarms. Any consequent changes in the stability and reliability of the fire protection system remain to be validated, especially in the complex and dynamic environment of buildings.

In terms of four-class confusion matrix metrics, the model-defined accuracy and the macro F1 are 92.55% and 92.73%, respectively. In the Critical reference class, the model labeled 23 out of 387 samples as High Risk. The persistence comparator yielded fewer samples downgraded to High Risk (19) despite having a higher MAE in forecasts. Therefore, predictive error and misclassification into severe categories need a dedicated analysis.

In the proposed governance procedure, those 23 downgrades raise an issue, as the label of High Risk issued by the model cannot override a Critical signal generated independently or other protection functions certified. Staff should analyze any contradictory indications and sound an alarm on any critical situation regardless of the advisory forecast.

Furthermore, it is reinforced with the use of formal rules of governance that foster the openness of the decision-making process. Each control act may be linked directly to a specific safety level and its regulation, which makes the work of the automated system more readable and more trustworthy.

In general, the findings indicate the hypothesis that the implementation of the governance decision rules may support the design of more steady, transparent, and reliable automated safety management as a part of the AI-based fire protection strategies.

sec.title: 8.4. Comparison with conventional fire protection systems
sec.p: The safety governance system proposed has certain functional differences from conventional fire alarm systems. The traditional systems have fixed levels such as predetermined temperature or smoke levels in order to trigger the alarms. These thresholds are simple to implement, and they do not necessarily aid in indicating the overall safety condition of the building particularly in instances where it comprises of a number of abnormal factors.

On the other hand, the proposed system is designed to evaluate model-derived conditions continuously by using an aggregate safety index based on multiple variables. The governance module is intended to recommend proposed actions based on quantitative limits rather than absolute thresholds through the application of real-time measurements, system reliability, and employing AI to anticipate future safety states. The single-temperature comparator uses a reference class derived from the multivariate index and is not an independent real-fire evaluation.

As shown, this solution is intended to support earlier consideration of changes in a model-defined index and more structured proposed decision-making. The visionary and predictive nature of the governance structure may inform proposed actions; their timing in actual fires was not tested.

The latter gains importance especially in smart buildings where the fire protection system is frequently self-contained and does not require much human oversight. The system could support operational safety through a quantitative and AI-based system of governance compared to standard systems of thresholds, subject to field validation.

sec.title: 8.5. Limitations of the proposed framework
sec.p: Although the suggested safety governance framework shows good performance, there are a number of limitations that need to be acknowledged.

First, the analysis presented in this study is based on hypothetical scenarios. The presence of a real-life smart building setting can cause further uncertainties, including unforeseen occupancy habits, environmental variations, or uncharacterized system behaviour, which might have an impact on the performance of the framework.

The next stage of the research involves validation of the framework using the data from smart buildings, optimizing the approach of weighting for different types of systems, as well as improving the predictive capabilities of AI.

sec.title: 8.6. Implications for smart building fire safety
sec.p: The proposed framework may provide a basis for future studies of governance workflows in smart buildings. Whether it improves coordination, fire detection, or emergency response in operational settings remains to be evaluated using data from actual buildings. Its applicability to other safety-critical building systems also requires further investigation.

sec.title: 9. Conclusion
sec.p: This study proposed a quantitative safety governance framework for AI-based fire-control systems in smart high-rise buildings. The framework combines a model-defined safety index, AI-based next-step prediction, and rule-based mapping of predicted conditions to governance levels and advisory control actions. Evaluation using synthetic scenarios demonstrates how this workflow operates under the assumptions specified in the study; it does not establish that the framework improves fire detection, reduces false alarms, accelerates emergency response, or increases safety in operational buildings. Its practical effectiveness and robustness should therefore be evaluated using data from real buildings and fire events, with particular attention to the quality of training data and the sensitivity of the safety index to its weighting coefficients.
